name: Dimethyl polysiloxane
text:
Dimethyl polysiloxane (PDMS) is a synthetic silicone polymer built from silicon, oxygen and methyl groups. It is made in grades ranging from a thin, clear liquid to a thick semi-solid.

In food it is used mainly as an anti-foaming agent and can also act as an anti-caking agent. It is added to many cooking and frying oils to stop foaming and splattering, so traces of it occur in some fried fast food.

A 2020 re-evaluation by the European Food Safety Authority found no safety concern for the reported uses, but recommended a maximum limit for cyclic siloxane impurities left over from manufacture.

name: Beeswax
text:
Beeswax is a natural wax produced by honey bees, which use it to build the cells of the honeycomb. For human use it comes mainly from the cappings cut off during honey extraction and from old comb. Yellow beeswax is the crude product; white beeswax is yellow wax that has been bleached or filtered.

In food it is used as a glazing agent that prevents water loss and protects the surface of some fruit. It is also used to coat cheese, in tablet coatings and soft capsules, and in chewing gum.

Humans digest it poorly, so it has no meaningful nutritional value. As an animal product it is not vegan.

name: Candelilla wax
text:
Candelilla wax is a natural plant wax obtained from the leaves and stems of the candelilla shrub (Euphorbia antisyphilitica), which is native to northern Mexico and the south-western United States. It is a hard, brittle, yellowish-brown wax.

In food it is used as a glazing agent. One of its main uses is as a binder in chewing gum, and it can replace carnauba wax or beeswax.

name: Carnauba wax
text:
Carnauba wax is a natural wax from the leaves of the carnauba palm (Copernicia prunifera), which grows only in north-eastern Brazil. The leaves are dried and beaten to loosen the wax, which is then refined and bleached. It has one of the highest melting points of any natural wax.

Because it gives a glossy finish, it is used as a glazing agent on foods such as sweets.

name: Shellac
text:
Shellac is a natural resin secreted by the female lac bug (Kerria lacca) on trees in the forests of India and Thailand. It is scraped from the bark, processed and sold as dry flakes.

In food and medicines it is used as a glazing agent, known as confectioner's glaze, on sweets and pills. It is also used as a coating on citrus fruit to extend storage life, and as part of the coating that replaces the natural wax removed from apples during cleaning.

As an insect product it is not vegan.

name: Microcrystalline wax
text:
Microcrystalline wax is a petroleum wax made by removing the oil from petrolatum during petroleum refining. It is a mixture of high-molecular-weight saturated hydrocarbons with more branched and ring-shaped molecules than paraffin wax. Its crystals are much finer, which makes it more flexible and sticky than paraffin wax, with a higher melting point.

In food it is used as a glazing agent and can also act as an anti-foaming agent.

name: Mineral oil, food grade
text:
Food-grade mineral oil is a highly refined, colourless and odourless liquid mixture of hydrocarbons (alkanes and cycloalkanes) obtained from petroleum.

It is used as a glazing and sealing agent. In confectionery it gives a glossy finish and keeps sweets from sticking together, and it is also used on machinery in the baking industry. Its use in food is self-limiting because it has a laxative effect.

name: Petrolatum (petroleum jelly)
text:
Petrolatum, better known as petroleum jelly (Vaseline is the best-known brand), is a semi-solid mixture of hydrocarbons obtained from petroleum.

In food it is classed as a glazing and sealing agent and as an anti-foaming agent.

name: Petroleum wax
text:
Petroleum wax is the group name for waxes obtained by refining petroleum. It covers microcrystalline wax and paraffin wax, mixtures of saturated hydrocarbons that are solid at room temperature.

They are used as glazing and sealing agents. Food-grade paraffin wax gives sweets a shiny coating, coats hard cheeses such as Edam, and is used in chewing gum. It is not digested and passes through the body unchanged.

name: Benzoin gum
text:
Benzoin gum (benzoin resin) is a balsamic resin obtained from the bark of several species of Styrax trees in South-East Asia. It has a sweet, vanilla-like aroma and is widely used in incense and perfumery. Its main active ingredient is benzoic acid.

As a food additive it is classed as a glazing agent. It is also used as a flavouring, for example in drinks, baked goods, chewing gum and sweets.

name: Hydrogenated poly-1-decene
text:
Hydrogenated poly-1-decene is a synthetic hydrocarbon made by polymerising the petrochemical 1-decene and then hydrogenating the product.

It is used as a glazing agent.

In a 2020 re-evaluation the European Food Safety Authority found it of low acute toxicity and not a genotoxicity concern, set an acceptable daily intake of 20 mg per kg of body weight, and concluded that its use at the maximum use levels does not raise a safety concern.

name: Rice bran wax
text:
Rice bran wax is an edible vegetable wax extracted from rice bran oil. It consists mainly of esters of long-chain fatty acids and higher alcohols. Because of its relatively high melting point it can replace carnauba wax in most applications.

It is used as a glazing agent. Its food uses include coatings for fruit and vegetables, confectionery and chewing gum.

name: Spermaceti wax
text:
Spermaceti is a waxy substance found in the head cavity of the sperm whale. It forms hard white crystals that are oily to the touch and have no taste or smell. Whalers extracted it from the 17th century onwards for candles, cosmetics and textiles.

As a food additive it is classed as a glazing agent. Jojoba esters, made from jojoba oil, are a plant-based wax that is chemically very similar.

name: Wax esters
text:
Wax esters are esters formed from one fatty acid and one long-chain fatty alcohol. They are the main components of carnauba wax and beeswax, and occur naturally in small amounts in foods such as whole-grain cereals, seeds, nuts, fish roe and some fish.

As a food additive they are classed as glazing agents.

name: Methyl esters of fatty acids
text:
Methyl esters of fatty acids are made by reacting fats or oils with methanol (transesterification). They are colourless compounds with melting points near room temperature, and are best known as the main components of biodiesel.

As a food additive they are classed as glazing agents. In the United States, methyl esters of fatty acids from edible fats and oils are used in a water emulsion when grapes are dried to make raisins.

name: Montan acid esters
text:
Montan acid esters are waxes made from montan wax, a hard fossil plant wax obtained by solvent extraction of certain types of lignite (brown coal).

They were used as glazing agents for the surface treatment of fruit. The EU had allowed them on citrus fruit, melons, papayas, mangoes, avocados and pineapples, but removed them from its list of food additives in 2014 (Regulation (EU) No 957/2014). The European Food Safety Authority had concluded in 2013 that it could not evaluate their safety because toxicity data were limited and no usage data had been submitted.

name: Lanolin
text:
Lanolin, or wool wax, is a wax secreted by the sebaceous glands of sheep and other wool-bearing animals. It is recovered when raw wool is washed with hot water and detergent. Chemically it consists mainly of sterol esters rather than true fats.

It is widely used in skin-care products and cosmetics. As a food additive it is classed as a glazing agent. A compound extracted from lanolin, 7-dehydrocholesterol, is a raw material for making vitamin D3.

name: Oxidised polyethylene wax
text:
Oxidised polyethylene wax is a synthetic wax made by oxidising polyethylene. It consists of oxidised long-chain acids, alcohols and esters.

It is used as a glazing agent for the surface treatment of some fruits.

In a 2015 re-evaluation the European Food Safety Authority found it not genotoxic. The data were insufficient to set an acceptable daily intake, but given the very low estimated intake the authority concluded that its current use is of no safety concern.

name: Esters of colophony
text:
Colophony, also called rosin, is a resin obtained from pine trees and other conifers, made up mainly of resin acids such as abietic acid. E915 covers its glycerol, methyl and pentaerythritol esters.

They are classed as glazing agents and are used in medicines and chewing gum. A related compound, glycerol ester of wood rosin (E445), is used as an emulsifier in soft drinks.

name: Calcium iodate
text:
Calcium iodate is the calcium salt of iodic acid, a colourless inorganic compound. It occurs naturally as the mineral lautarite, the most important mineral source of iodine, which is mined in the Atacama Desert.

As a food additive it is classed as a flour treatment agent. It is also used as an iodine supplement in chicken feed.

name: Potassium iodate
text:
Potassium iodate (KIO3) is the potassium salt of iodic acid, a white, water-soluble salt and an oxidising agent.

As a food additive it is classed as a flour treatment agent and is occasionally used as a maturing agent in baking. It is also used in some countries to iodise table salt against iodine deficiency, and to supply iodine in some infant formulas.

name: Nitrogen oxides
text:
Nitrogen oxides are compounds made only of nitrogen and oxygen, such as nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2).

As a food additive they are classed as flour treatment agents.

name: Nitrosyl chloride
text:
Nitrosyl chloride (NOCl) is a yellow gas and a strong oxidising agent. It can be made by combining chlorine with nitric oxide and is a component of aqua regia, the mixture of hydrochloric and nitric acids.

As a food additive it is classed as a flour treatment agent.

name: L-cysteine
text:
L-cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid found in proteins. Most of it is made by hydrolysis of animal materials such as poultry feathers or hog hair; human hair is rarely used, and EU law does not allow it as a source. A more expensive version made by fermentation is also available.

In food it is a flour treatment agent used as a processing aid in baking: small amounts soften dough and shorten processing time. It is also used to make meat flavourings.

When it comes from animal sources it is not suitable for vegan, vegetarian, kosher or halal diets.

name: L-cystine
text:
L-cystine is formed from two molecules of the amino acid cysteine joined by a disulfide bond. It is a white solid that dissolves poorly in water. It is common in foods such as eggs, meat, dairy products and whole grains, and in skin, horn and hair; human hair is about 10 to 14 percent cystine by mass.

As a food additive it is classed as a flour treatment agent.

name: Potassium persulfate
text:
Potassium persulfate (potassium peroxydisulfate, K2S2O8) is a white inorganic salt that dissolves poorly in cold water and better in warm water. It is a powerful oxidising agent.

As a food additive it is classed as a flour treatment agent. Industrially it is mainly used to start the polymerisation of plastics and synthetic rubber, and it is also used in hair bleaches.

name: Ammonium persulfate
text:
Ammonium persulfate ((NH4)2S2O8) is a colourless or white inorganic salt that dissolves readily in water. It is a strong oxidising agent.

As a food additive it is classed as a flour treatment agent. Industrially it is used to start polymerisation reactions, to etch copper on printed circuit boards, and as a cleaning and bleaching agent.

name: Potassium bromate
text:
Potassium bromate (KBrO3) is a colourless salt and a strong oxidising agent. It has been used as a flour improver that strengthens dough and helps bread rise higher. During baking it is normally reduced to bromide, but if too much is added or the bread is underbaked, some may remain in the product.

The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies it as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B). In the United States the FDA has urged bakers not to use it since 1991, and California passed a law in 2023 prohibiting it from 2027.

name: Calcium bromate
text:
Calcium bromate (Ca(BrO3)2) is the calcium salt of bromic acid, usually found as the monohydrate. Like potassium bromate (E924), it is a bromate.

In some countries it is used as a flour and bread dough improver (conditioner).

name: Chlorine
text:
Chlorine is a chemical element that forms a yellow-green, poisonous gas at room temperature. It is extremely reactive and a strong oxidising agent, so in nature it occurs only in compounds such as table salt. It is produced commercially from brine by electrolysis.

As a food additive it is classed as a flour treatment agent used to bleach flour. It is much more widely used to disinfect drinking water and swimming pools and to make bleaches.

name: Chlorine dioxide
text:
Chlorine dioxide (ClO2) is a yellowish-green gas above 11 °C and is usually handled as a solution in water. It is a strong oxidiser, commonly used as a bleach and disinfectant, for example to bleach wood pulp and to disinfect drinking water.

As a food additive it is classed as a flour treatment agent and has been used to bleach flour; it is also used for disinfection in food processing. It is toxic, so limits on human exposure apply.

name: Azodicarbonamide
text:
Azodicarbonamide is a synthetic yellow to orange-red, odourless crystalline powder. Its main use is as a blowing agent that makes foamed plastics.

In food it is used in some countries as a flour bleaching agent and dough conditioner. It reacts with moist flour; the main product, biurea, is stable during baking, and small amounts of semicarbazide and ethyl carbamate also form. Semicarbazide shows weak carcinogenic activity in laboratory animals, but human data are inconclusive.

In 2012 it was added to the EU's REACH candidate list of substances of very high concern because it can cause respiratory sensitisation in workers who handle it.

name: Carbamide
text:
Carbamide, better known as urea (CO(NH2)2), is a colourless, odourless solid that dissolves readily in water. It is the main nitrogen-containing substance in mammalian urine and is formed in the liver from ammonia and carbon dioxide. Industrially it is made from synthetic ammonia and carbon dioxide, and over 90 percent of production goes into fertilisers.

As a food additive it is classed as a flour treatment agent; in the EU its listed use is in chewing gum without added sugar. It is also used as a yeast nutrient in fermenting sugars into alcohol.

name: Benzoyl peroxide
text:
Benzoyl peroxide is a synthetic organic peroxide, a white granular solid with a faint smell of benzaldehyde that dissolves poorly in water. It is an oxidiser used mainly in making plastics and for bleaching flour, hair and textiles. It is also a common acne medication.

As a food additive it is classed as a bleaching agent, flour treatment agent and preservative.

name: Acetone peroxide
text:
Acetone peroxide is an organic peroxide formed by reacting acetone with hydrogen peroxide in the presence of an acid catalyst. In pure form it is a sensitive explosive that can detonate from heat, friction or shock.

In food it has been used as a flour treatment agent, to bleach and mature flour.

name: Calcium peroxide
text:
Calcium peroxide is an inorganic compound with the formula CaO2. The pure substance is white; commercial samples can be yellowish. It is almost insoluble in water and releases oxygen when it comes into contact with water.

In food it is used as a flour treatment agent, bleaching and improving flour.

name: Argon
text:
Argon is an inert noble gas that makes up about 0.93% of the Earth's atmosphere. It is obtained industrially by fractional distillation of liquefied air.

In food it is used as a packaging gas: it displaces air containing oxygen and moisture from packs, slowing oxidation and other reactions that spoil the product. In winemaking it is used to keep oxygen away from the surface of the wine.

name: Helium
text:
Helium is a light, colourless, odourless, non-toxic and inert noble gas. Commercially it is extracted from natural gas, which can contain up to about 7% helium, by fractional distillation.

In food it is used as a packaging gas and propellant.

name: Dichlorodifluoromethane
text:
Dichlorodifluoromethane (R-12, sold as Freon-12) is a colourless chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) gas, used in the past as a refrigerant and aerosol propellant. In food it was listed as a propellant.

It strongly depletes the ozone layer. Under the Montreal Protocol its manufacture was phased out in developed countries in 1996 and in developing countries in 2010.

name: Nitrogen
text:
Nitrogen is a colourless, odourless, inert gas that makes up about 78% of the air. It is produced industrially by fractional distillation of liquid air or by separating it from air mechanically.

About two thirds of commercially produced nitrogen is used as an oxygen-free gas, for example in food packaging. Alone or mixed with carbon dioxide, it keeps packaged foods fresh by delaying rancidity and oxidation. It is also used to pressurise kegs of some beers, especially stouts, giving smaller bubbles.

name: Nitrous oxide
text:
Nitrous oxide (N2O), commonly known as laughing gas, is a colourless, non-flammable gas with a faint sweet smell. In medicine it is used for its anaesthetic and pain-reducing effects.

In food it is mainly a propellant for aerosol whipped cream: the gas dissolves in the fatty cream under pressure and expands into foam when the cream leaves the can. It is also used in cooking sprays.

name: Butane
text:
Butane is a highly flammable, colourless hydrocarbon gas that is easily liquefied under pressure. It occurs in natural gas and is a component of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

In food it is used as a propellant. Under EU rules this use is limited to vegetable oil pan sprays for professional use, water-based emulsion sprays, and certain colour preparations for professional use.

name: Isobutane
text:
Isobutane (2-methylpropane) is a colourless, odourless, flammable hydrocarbon gas, an isomer of butane. It is obtained by isomerisation of butane.

In food it is used as a propellant. Under EU rules this use is limited to vegetable oil pan sprays for professional use, water-based emulsion sprays, and certain colour preparations for professional use.

name: Propane
text:
Propane is a flammable hydrocarbon gas, a by-product of natural gas processing and petroleum refining, widely used as a fuel in liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). It is easily liquefied under pressure.

In food it is used as a propellant. Under EU rules this use is limited to vegetable oil pan sprays for professional use, water-based emulsion sprays, and certain colour preparations for professional use.

name: Chloropentafluoroethane
text:
Chloropentafluoroethane (R-115, CFC-115) is a chlorofluorocarbon gas once used as a refrigerant. As a food additive it was listed as a propellant.

Because of its high ozone depletion potential and very long lifetime in the environment, its production and consumption were phased out from 1 January 1996 under the Montreal Protocol. It is also a potent greenhouse gas.

name: Octafluorocyclobutane
text:
Octafluorocyclobutane (perfluorocyclobutane, C4F8) is a colourless, chemically inert gas, the fully fluorinated analogue of cyclobutane. It is made from tetrafluoroethylene and is used mainly in semiconductor manufacturing.

Because it is volatile and inert, it may be found as a propellant in some aerosol foods.

name: Oxygen
text:
Oxygen is a colourless, odourless and tasteless gas that makes up about 21% of the atmosphere. Industrially it is usually obtained by fractional distillation of liquefied air.

In food it is used as a packaging gas. In modified-atmosphere packs of red meat, high oxygen levels (around 80%) are used to keep the meat bright red. For most other foods, oxygen is reduced or replaced in the pack, because it speeds up spoilage.

name: Hydrogen
text:
Hydrogen is the lightest element; as a gas it is colourless, odourless and highly flammable. Almost all of it is produced from fossil fuels, mainly by steam reforming of natural gas; it can also be made by electrolysis of water.

In food it is used as a packaging gas and also has antioxidant properties. Separately, hydrogen is used to convert unsaturated fats and oils into saturated ones by hydrogenation.

name: Acesulfame K
text:
Acesulfame potassium (acesulfame K) is a synthetic, calorie-free sweetener, a white crystalline powder about 200 times sweeter than sugar. Like saccharin, it can leave a slightly bitter aftertaste at high concentrations.

Unlike aspartame, it is stable to heat, so it can be used in baking and in products with a long shelf life. It is often blended with other sweeteners, usually sucralose or aspartame, to give a more sugar-like taste.

name: Aspartame
text:
Aspartame is a synthetic sweetener about 180 to 200 times sweeter than sugar, the methyl ester of a dipeptide of aspartic acid and phenylalanine.

It is used in diet soft drinks, chewing gum and tabletop sweeteners, but breaks down at high temperatures.

Aspartame is a source of phenylalanine, which people with phenylketonuria cannot properly metabolise, so EU labels must state that the food contains a source of phenylalanine.

In 2023 IARC classified aspartame as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B) on limited evidence. At the same time JECFA, the FAO/WHO expert committee on food additives, saw no reason to change the acceptable daily intake of 40 mg/kg body weight.

name: Cyclamates
text:
Cyclamates are the sodium and calcium salts of cyclamic acid. They are synthetic sweeteners 30 to 50 times sweeter than sugar, the least potent of the commercial artificial sweeteners. They are cheap and heat-stable, so they can be used in cooking and baking.

Cyclamate is often mixed with saccharin, commonly 10 parts to 1, which masks the off-tastes of both.

In the United States cyclamate was withdrawn from foods in 1969 and 1970 after a study linked the cyclamate–saccharin mixture to bladder cancer in rats; the FDA has since stated that the evidence does not implicate cyclamate as a carcinogen.

name: Isomalt
text:
Isomalt is a sugar alcohol (polyol) made from sucrose, usually from sugar beet: an enzyme first converts sucrose to isomaltulose, which is then hydrogenated. It is less sweet than sugar and provides 2 kcal per gram, half as much as sugar. It has little effect on blood sugar and does not promote tooth decay.

It is widely used in sugar-free sweets, especially hard-boiled candy, because it resists crystallisation.

It is incompletely absorbed and can cause diarrhoea and flatulence. EU labels of foods with more than 10% added polyols must state that excessive consumption may produce laxative effects.

name: Saccharin
text:
Saccharin, first produced in 1879, is a calorie-free synthetic sweetener about 500 times sweeter than sugar. It is mostly used as its sodium salt; the calcium salt is used by people limiting sodium. It is heat-stable but can leave a bitter or metallic aftertaste.

It sweetens drinks, sweets and baked goods and masks the bitter taste of some medicines.

In the 1970s high doses caused bladder cancer in rats. Later research found the mechanism specific to rats, and epidemiological studies showed no link in humans; IARC moved saccharin from Group 2B to Group 3, and in 2000 the US dropped its warning label.

name: Sucralose
text:
Sucralose (trichlorogalactosucrose) is a synthetic sweetener made by chlorinating sucrose, replacing three of its hydroxyl groups with chlorine. It is about 600 times sweeter than sugar. Most ingested sucralose is not absorbed and is excreted in the faeces.

At normal baking temperatures it is mostly heat-stable and keeps its sweetness, so it is used in baked goods. When heated above about 120 °C, chlorinated organic compounds can form in unknown amounts.

name: Alitame
text:
Alitame is a synthetic dipeptide sweetener made from aspartic acid and alanine, developed by Pfizer in the early 1980s and marketed in some countries as Aclame. It is about 2,000 times sweeter than sugar and has no aftertaste.

It is more stable under hot or acidic conditions than aspartame. Unlike aspartame it contains no phenylalanine, so it can be used by people with phenylketonuria.

name: Thaumatin
text:
Thaumatin is a mixture of intensely sweet proteins first isolated from the fruit of the West African katemfe plant (Thaumatococcus daniellii), which has long been used locally to flavour foods and drinks.

It is a low-calorie sweetener and taste modifier, often used more for its flavour-modifying properties than as a sweetener. Its sweetness lasts a long time and at high concentrations leaves a liquorice-like aftertaste.

name: Glycyrrhizin
text:
Glycyrrhizin (glycyrrhizic acid) is the main sweet-tasting constituent of liquorice root (Glycyrrhiza glabra), obtained as an extract by soaking and boiling the root in water. It is 30 to 50 times sweeter than sugar.

It is used as a sweetener and flavour enhancer. Regular consumption of black liquorice can lower blood potassium and raise blood pressure. In the EU, confectionery and drinks containing glycyrrhizinic acid above set levels must be labelled 'contains liquorice', and at higher levels must add that people with hypertension should avoid excessive consumption.

name: Neohesperidine DC
text:
Neohesperidine dihydrochalcone (NHDC) is a sweetener made from citrus: neohesperidin, a bitter compound extracted from bitter orange, is treated with a strong base and hydrogenated. It is about 1,500 to 1,800 times sweeter than sugar at threshold concentrations and around 340 times at higher ones. Its sweetness starts slowly and lingers.

It is used as a flavour enhancer and sweetener, especially to mask bitterness, including in tablets and in livestock feed. It works synergistically with other sweeteners.

name: Steviol glycosides
text:
Steviol glycosides, such as stevioside and rebaudioside A, are the compounds that give the leaves of the South American plant Stevia rebaudiana their sweet taste. Reported sweetness ranges from 30 to 320 times that of sugar; a recent evaluation put rebaudioside A at about 240 times and stevioside at about 140 times. Rebaudioside A had the least bitterness and aftertaste.

The acceptable daily intake is 4 mg per kg of body weight, expressed as steviol. The EU now lists them as E960a to E960d: extracted from stevia, from fermentation, enzymatically produced, and glucosylated.

name: Neotame
text:
Neotame is a non-caloric artificial sweetener, an analogue of aspartame. By mass it is 7,000 to 13,000 times sweeter than sugar, so only tiny amounts are needed. It is chemically somewhat more stable than aspartame.

It is used as a sweetener and flavour enhancer. Neotame can form phenylalanine in the body, but at normal levels of use this is not significant for people with phenylketonuria.

name: Aspartame-acesulfame salt
text:
Aspartame-acesulfame salt, marketed as Twinsweet, is a synthetic sweetener made by soaking a 2:1 mixture of aspartame and acesulfame potassium in an acidic solution and letting it crystallise; moisture and potassium are removed in the process. It is about 350 times sweeter than sugar.

It is used as a sweetener. Because it contains aspartame, a source of phenylalanine, EU labels must state that the food contains a source of phenylalanine.

name: Polyglycitol syrup
text:
Polyglycitol syrup, also called hydrogenated starch hydrolysates, is a mixture of sugar alcohols such as sorbitol, maltitol and longer-chain hydrogenated saccharides. It is made by partly breaking down starch, most often corn starch, and then hydrogenating it. It is 40 to 90% as sweet as sugar.

It is used like other polyols, often blended with other sweeteners, and prevents sugar crystals forming in syrups. Oral bacteria do not readily ferment it, so it does not promote tooth decay. In large amounts it is laxative; EU labels of foods with more than 10% added polyols must say so.

name: Maltitol
text:
Maltitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) made by hydrogenating maltose obtained from starch. It has 75 to 90% of the sweetness of sugar and provides 2 to 3 kcal per gram. It does not promote tooth decay. Maltitol syrup, made by hydrogenating corn syrup, contains 50 to 80% maltitol.

It is used in sugar-free hard candy, chewing gum, chocolate, baked goods and ice cream. It is largely fermented by gut bacteria and has a laxative effect; EU labels of foods with more than 10% added polyols must warn that excessive consumption may produce laxative effects.

name: Lactitol
text:
Lactitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) made by hydrogenating lactose, the sugar of milk. It has 30 to 40% of the sweetness of sugar and about 60% of its calories. It does not promote tooth decay or raise blood glucose.

It is used as a bulk sweetener in sugar-free sweets, biscuits, chocolate and ice cream. Most of it reaches the large intestine, where it draws in water; it is also used medically as a laxative. EU labels of foods with more than 10% added polyols must warn that excessive consumption may produce laxative effects.

name: Xylitol
text:
Xylitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol), sometimes called birch sugar because it can be extracted from birch wood. Industrially, xylose is obtained from plant material such as wood or maize waste and then hydrogenated. It is about as sweet as sugar with 40% fewer calories and has negligible effect on blood sugar.

It is used in chewing gum, sweets, toothpaste and medicines. High doses can cause flatulence and diarrhoea; EU labels of foods with more than 10% added polyols must warn of laxative effects. Xylitol is poisonous to dogs.

name: Erythritol
text:
Erythritol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) found in small amounts in some fruits and fermented foods. It is produced from corn using enzymes and fermentation. It is 60 to 70% as sweet as sugar, almost calorie-free, does not affect blood sugar and does not cause tooth decay. It has a strong cooling effect when it dissolves.

About 90% is absorbed and excreted unchanged in urine, so small doses rarely cause the bloating typical of other polyols. In 2023 EFSA set an acceptable daily intake of 0.5 g per kg of body weight, to protect against its laxative effect.

name: Advantame
text:
Advantame is a non-caloric artificial sweetener developed by Ajinomoto, an analogue of aspartame that can be made from aspartame and vanillin. By mass it is about 20,000 times sweeter than sugar and about 110 times sweeter than aspartame. It is chemically more stable than aspartame and has no notable off-flavours.

It is used as a sweetener and flavour enhancer. It can form phenylalanine in the body, but at normal levels of use this is not significant for people with phenylketonuria.

name: Quillaia extract
text:
Quillaia extract is obtained from the milled inner bark or small stems and branches of the soapbark tree (Quillaja saponaria). It contains high concentrations of saponins, along with tannins and other polyphenols.

In food it is used as a foaming agent in soft drinks and as an emulsifier. Highly purified quillaia saponins are also used as adjuvants in some veterinary and human vaccines.
